title: Mitsui's Cash and Fixed Prices
text:
In 1673 Mitsui Takatoshi, a merchant from Matsusaka, opened a kimono fabric shop called Echigoya in Edo, the city that is now Tokyo. The trade was dominated by established houses that served wealthy customers in a particular way. Clerks carried samples to clients' homes, prices were bargained case by case, and goods were sold on credit, with bills settled once or twice a year. The system was slow and costly, and the merchants built the risk of unpaid debts into their prices.

Takatoshi turned this around. Customers came to the shop, where prices were set and displayed, with no haggling and no credit: payment in cash on the spot. Because he was not carrying debts for months, he could charge less. He also sold cloth cut to whatever length a customer wanted, so people of modest means could buy what they needed rather than a whole bolt.

The established merchants were hostile and tried to obstruct him, but customers flocked to Echigoya. Its trade grew rapidly, and in the 1680s Takatoshi moved to a larger site and added a money exchange business that later served the shogunate. The shop became the ancestor of the Mitsukoshi department store, and the family business grew into the Mitsui group.
lesson: Look at the hidden costs and frictions everyone in your field accepts as normal. Removing them for the customer can be a more powerful advantage than a better product.
source: Mitsui corporate histories; Charles David Sheldon, The Rise of the Merchant Class in Tokugawa Japan (1958)
caveat: Sources differ on whether the cash and fixed price policy began at the opening in 1673 or was formalized a few years later.
